name: Boeing EA-18G Growler
operator: U.S. Navy; Royal Australian Air Force (only export operator)
overview_md:
The EA-18G Growler is the West's premier airborne electronic-attack aircraft — a Super Hornet derivative built to jam enemy radars and communications, suppress and destroy air defences, and protect strike packages in contested airspace. It is included in an Indo-Pacific reference both as a U.S. Navy carrier-air-wing mainstay and because the Royal Australian Air Force is the only operator outside the United States, making it a distinctly allied Indo-Pacific capability.

Built on the two-seat F/A-18F airframe, the Growler retains much of the Super Hornet's flight performance while adding a powerful electronic-warfare suite: jamming pods (the legacy ALQ-99 being replaced by the more capable Next Generation Jammer), receivers to locate and characterise enemy emitters, and the AGM-88 HARM/AARGM anti-radiation missile to physically destroy radars. It can blind an integrated air-defence system, deny enemy communications and escort strike aircraft through defended airspace.

For an analyst, the Growler is a critical enabler in any high-end fight — the aircraft that makes a modern integrated air-defence system penetrable. Australia's operation of the type gives the U.S.-allied coalition a shared, interoperable electronic-attack capability in the Pacific, and the platform's role only grows as adversary air defences like the HQ-9 and S-400 proliferate. Electronic warfare is often the decisive, invisible layer of air combat, and the Growler is how the West fights it.

additional.ew_suite: ALQ-99 jamming pods (Next Generation Jammer replacing)

combat_history.event: Used in U.S. operations (Libya, Iraq/Syria) for electronic attack and SEAD support.
combat_history.significance: Proven enabler for strike operations against air defences.

modernization.description: Replacing the legacy ALQ-99 with a far more capable jamming system.
modernization.impact: Sharply improves electronic-attack reach and effectiveness.

vulnerabilities.description: A 4.5-gen airframe with a large signature.
vulnerabilities.context: Vulnerable to modern fighters/SAMs if unsupported.

vulnerabilities.description: Specialised, expensive aircraft in limited numbers.

operational_patterns.typical_deployment: Electronic attack and SEAD escorting strike packages through contested airspace; carrier and land-based.
operational_patterns.typical_task_group: U.S. carrier air wings; RAAF strike packages with F-35A and Super Hornet.

peer_comparisons.key_differences: China's electronic-attack Flanker variant performs the same jamming/SEAD role for the PLA.
peer_comparisons.video_angle: The electronic-attack aircraft of the Pacific.

peer_comparisons.key_differences: The Growler is the EW-specialised version of the Super Hornet.
peer_comparisons.video_angle: How the Super Hornet became an EW jet.

peer_comparisons.key_differences: The KJ-500 enables (early warning); the Growler disables (jamming) — opposite sides of the EW fight.

doctrine.role: Airborne electronic-attack aircraft — jam and destroy enemy air defences and protect strike packages.
doctrine.employment: Stand-off and escort jamming with HARM/AARGM anti-radiation missiles to blind and kill radars.
doctrine.design_philosophy: Make integrated air defences penetrable — the invisible enabling layer of air combat.
doctrine.threat_context: Allied (US + RAAF) electronic attack against proliferating HQ-9/S-400-class defences in the Pacific.
doctrine.comparison_frame: Read against China's J-16D, the base Super Hornet and (as its opposite) the KJ-500.
